origin_region: Nantou, Chiayi · Alishan, Taitung and New Taipei · Pinglin (small producers island-wide)
cultivar: Qingxin, Jin Xuan, Si Ji Chun, Da Ye oolong or Qingxin Damou, depending on the maker
processing: Withered for a long time indoors or in gentle sun with no rolling and no pan-firing, then dried at low temperature; some lots use leafhopper-bitten summer leaf, and some are pressed into small cakes after drying.
harvest_season: Spring buds and young leaf for the finer bud-heavy lots; bug-bitten summer leaf for honey-leaning lots; a few winter lots from Alishan.
appearance_dry: Loose, fluffy, unrolled leaves in mixed greens, greys and browns with downy silver buds, very light in the hand.
appearance_wet: Whole, soft leaves and buds in greenish brown, barely changed in shape.
taste_profile: Hay, honey and white flowers with a light, sweet, slightly cooling body; bug-bitten lots lean to honey and dried apricot.

brewing.notes: Fill the gaiwan well because the leaf is bulky, and give it longer steeps than an oolong. Also suits a big glass of hot water left to stand, and cold-brews into a clean, sweet drink.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's tea by maker, in small quantities and at prices from modest to surprising, with the cultivar and picking stated if the maker is serious; a few pressed cakes are offered with three to five years of age in the hope that they develop like Fujian white tea. There are no established grades and competitions are rare.
description:
Taiwanese white tea is a new thing. Taiwan has no white-tea tradition; what exists has been made since the 2010s by small producers in Nantou, Alishan, Taitung and the Pinglin hills looking for a new product, often with encouragement from the Tea Research and Extension Station, and it is made from oolong and black-tea cultivars rather than the Fujian white-tea bushes, so it tastes like nothing from Fuding.

The method is the simple one: leaf is picked, withered for a long time indoors or in gentle sun with no rolling and no pan-firing, and dried at low temperature. What goes in varies: spring buds and young leaf of Qing Xin or Jin Xuan for a Taiwanese 'silver needle' or Bai Mu Dan style, leafhopper-bitten summer leaf of Da Ye oolong or Qing Xin Da Mou for a honey-leaning style, and some makers press the finished leaf into small cakes in the hope that it ages like Fujian white tea.

The cup is pale and soft: hay, honey and white flowers with a light, sweet, slightly cooling body, and in the bug-bitten lots honey and dried apricot. It is gentle rather than complex. Brew it at around 85 degrees with the gaiwan well filled, because the leaf is bulky, and give it longer steeps than an oolong; it also suits a big glass of hot water left to stand, and it cold-brews into a clean, sweet drink.

It is sold as the current year's tea by maker, usually in small quantities and at prices that range from modest to surprising, with the cultivar and picking stated if the maker is serious; a few pressed cakes are offered with three to five years of age. There are no established grades and competitions are rare, so buy a small amount first.

If you want a reference point, drink it next to a Fujian Bai Mu Dan: the Taiwanese tea is sweeter and more floral, the Fujian one deeper and more savoury.
sources_note: That production started in the 2010s is approximate; a few makers may have experimented earlier. Cultivar mix varies widely by producer.
